mappings.note: Assertion and reason both concern a closed switch completing the path so current flows: an explanation of circuit behaviour.
Names the electric cell as the portable source of electrical energy, identification of a component by its function.
Counts a cell's two terminals. Part of the component-recall cluster this chapter houses in LO-17.
The metal cap as the positive terminal, identified from what can be seen on the cell.
The metal disc as the negative terminal, the companion identification.
Battery as the name for a group of cells. Naming, not the connection rule, so LO-17 rather than LO-21.
Names the filament inside an incandescent lamp.
That LEDs have no filament is only meaningful against the incandescent lamp that does, so this is the differentiation outcome rather than plain identification.
The longer lead as the LED's positive terminal: identification from an observable feature.
The electrical circuit as what provides a complete path for current. The circuit concept, so LO-22, not LO-25, where it would be drawn.
Fused as the term for a lamp stopped by a broken filament; the word carries the cause of the failure, which is why it sits with LO-21 rather than the identification cluster.
Names the switch from its job of completing or breaking a circuit: identification by function. The mirror-image item, which asks what a switch does, is on LO-22.
Matches the ON position to the closed state of the circuit, part of explaining when current flows.
Circuit diagram as the name for a symbol representation of a circuit.
The long line of the cell symbol: diagram convention, not a feature of the physical cell.
Names the conductor class. Category naming, so LO-19 rather than LO-18.
Names the insulator class, the companion category item.
Copper named as a wire material because it conducts: a material chosen on a property. Not LO-19, since no class is being defined.
Plastic or rubber named specifically as the covering used for safety, which is the everyday application of insulation rather than a bare material fact.
Places the human body in the conductor class. Classification only; the item asking why the body conducts sits on LO-21.
Batteries supply direct current: which kind of current comes from where, part of explaining the phenomenon rather than sorting materials.
Why electricity must be handled carefully and why only cells are used in experiments: safety practice in daily life. Not LO-32, since no value of honesty or objectivity is at issue.
Explains the positive-to-negative rule that makes a battery out of cells, the arrangement on which the result depends.
Describes the metal case and central tip as the lamp's two terminals: identification of parts from inspection.
Current heats the filament until it glows, which is the heating effect of electric current named verbatim in LO-22. Not LO-21, because a general mechanism is explained rather than one case diagnosed.
The longer and shorter leads of one LED tell its terminals apart, an observable feature of a single component. Not LO-18, which in this chapter covers contrasts between two devices or materials.
The LED glows only with matching polarity because current passes one way: the behaviour is traced to its cause.
The purpose of a switch, controlling current by closing or breaking the path: circuit behaviour explained.
Open against closed circuit is a contrast between two states of a circuit, not between materials, so LO-22 rather than LO-18.
Why standard symbols are used to draw circuits: the diagram convention and its purpose.
Reads the battery symbol as repeated cell symbols with long and short lines: symbol interpretation.
Conductors against insulators with an example of each, the differentiation LO-18 names explicitly.

Copper is chosen for wires because it conducts well; the reason rests on the material property. The safety-covering item next to it is on LO-29, where the everyday practice rather than the property is the answer.
Plastic and rubber coverings protect people from shocks: the insulator concept applied to everyday safety.
A fused lamp fails because the broken filament opens the circuit: symptom traced to cause.
Describes how to run the tester on a material and read the lamp: the investigation procedure, not the classification it yields.
Conventional current from positive to negative, part of how current flow is described and explained.
The metal strip in a compartment joins positive to negative so the cells act in series: how the required arrangement is achieved.
Why a torch lights in only one switch position: closed path against broken path. General circuit behaviour, so LO-22.
AC and DC distinguished by source and use. LO-18 is unavailable for this since it covers materials and organisms.
The plus and minus markings exist so terminals can be told apart and the cell inserted the right way round: identification by a marked feature.
Five-mark item that both names the torch's parts (LO-17) and explains how switching completes the path and lights the lamp (LO-22). Both halves are required by the question.
Asks for the circuit to be drawn in standard symbols (LO-25) on the back of assembling it with a home-made switch (LO-27). Both are in the expected answer.
Compares incandescent lamp and LED across structure, terminals and how light is produced: the fullest differentiation item in the chapter.
Run the tester over five objects (LO-20) and then place each in the conductor or insulator class with a reason (LO-19). Both the doing and the sorting carry marks.
Four switch combinations, each justified by which branch is complete: outcomes tied to circuit states throughout.
Series cells are not enough because the LED's polarity must also match; two causes must be handled together. Not LO-25, since the figure is referred to but nothing is drawn.

Where conductors and insulators are each needed in real appliances and wiring: the concept applied to daily life. Not LO-18, because the item asks for uses rather than for the two classes to be told apart.

Proposes two fresh groupings for the listed uses of electricity, which is building a classification rather than applying one. Not LO-31, because the creativity is in the categories, not in a design made from materials.
Lists four candidate causes for a dead circuit. Diagnosis only, so LO-21; the earlier item that also asked how to find the fault is on LO-20.
With cells and lamp known good, the fault is pinned on the switch or the cell seating: another effect-to-cause diagnosis.
Whether direction matters after swapping an LED for an incandescent lamp turns on the difference between the two devices, so LO-18 rather than LO-21.

Pure water as a poor conductor and salt water as a conductor is a property-based discrimination between two samples. Not LO-19, because no class is being named, and not LO-20, since the result is predicted rather than measured.
Making the LED brighter by adding a cell to the battery relates the observed brightness to the source. Not LO-25, because the diagram belongs to an earlier part of the case study.

With bulb and battery excluded, the switch is the remaining component that could have failed: elimination of causes. Not LO-22, because one broken device is being found rather than the circuit explained.
